concepts.caption: An umbrella over what you already own. You keep the stock - the put absorbs the crash.
concepts.definition: Insurance on a bet you already have.
concepts.example: You own $100,000 of stock and buy a put so a crash hurts less.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A hedge protects what you own. A pledge puts it up as collateral.

concepts.caption: You keep the shares, but they are on a leash: miss the loan and the bank takes them.
concepts.definition: Put an asset up so a lender can take it if you don't pay.
concepts.example: You pledge $1M of stock for a $700k loan. You still own the stock — until you don't pay.
concepts.mixUpWhy: You still own it. Pledge = collateral. Sell = it's gone.

concepts.caption: The pile the lender is allowed to grab if you stop paying.
concepts.definition: The thing the lender can seize if you skip payments.
concepts.example: The pledged stock is the collateral. Miss the loan, the bank takes the shares.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Collateral is the asset. The haircut is how much they knock off its value before lending.

concepts.caption: The discount: $1M of stock gets treated as $700k before anyone lends a cent.
concepts.definition: The discount a lender applies to collateral before they'll lend against it.
concepts.example: $1M stock, 30% haircut → they treat it as $700k. That's the max loan.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Haircut is the discount on collateral. Margin is the cash cushion you must keep.

concepts.caption: The cash cushion that has to stay in the account while the bet sits on top.
concepts.definition: Cash or equity you must keep in the account as a cushion.
concepts.example: Broker lets you buy $10k of stock with $5k cash. That $5k is margin.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Margin is the cushion. Leverage is the size of the bet that cushion supports.

concepts.caption: The phone rings when the cushion is gone: post more cash, or get sold out.
concepts.definition: The lender demanding more cash — or selling you out — because the cushion got too thin.
concepts.example: Stock drops 40%. Collateral is now $600k against a $700k loan. The bank calls.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The haircut was set at the start. A margin call happens later, when prices move against you.

concepts.caption: A small pile of your own cash holding up a much bigger bet.
concepts.definition: Using borrowed money or derivatives to make a bigger bet than your cash.
concepts.example: $10k of yours plus $40k borrowed = 5× leverage. A 10% drop wipes half your cash.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Leverage is the multiplier. Margin is the cushion that makes the multiplier possible.

concepts.caption: The contract is not the thing - its value just comes from the thing.
concepts.definition: A contract whose value comes from something else — a stock, a rate, a barrel of oil.
concepts.example: A put on Apple is a derivative. The put is not Apple stock; it just bets on Apple's price.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An option is one kind of derivative. Futures and swaps are derivatives too.

concepts.caption: A ticket you can tear up: the right to buy or sell, never the duty.
concepts.definition: The right, not the obligation, to buy or sell something at a set price.
concepts.example: Pay $3 for the right to sell a $100 stock at $90. That's an option. You can walk away.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An option you can abandon. A futures contract you must settle.

concepts.caption: The right to sell at a floor price. It pays when the price falls.
concepts.definition: An option to sell at a set price. Pays off when the thing falls.
concepts.example: Stock at $100. A $90 put pays if it drops below $90. Crash insurance if you own it.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Put = right to sell (you want it down). Call = right to buy (you want it up).

concepts.caption: The right to buy at a set price. It pays when the price rises.
concepts.definition: An option to buy at a set price. Pays off when the thing rises.
concepts.example: Stock at $100. A $110 call pays if it rips above $110. That's a bullish bet.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Call = right to buy (up). Put = right to sell (down).

concepts.caption: Sell borrowed shares today, buy them back tomorrow - cheaper, you hope.
concepts.definition: Borrow shares, sell them now, hope to buy back cheaper later.
concepts.example: Borrow 100 shares, sell at $50, buy back at $30, return them. You keep $20. If it goes to $80, you owe.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A put is a limited-loss down bet. A short can lose without a ceiling if the stock rips.

concepts.caption: A wide exit: you can sell fast without shoving the price around.
concepts.definition: How fast you can sell without moving the price much.
concepts.example: Apple stock is liquid — dump $1M and the price barely budges. Your cousin's startup is not.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Liquidity is ease of exit. Notional is the face size of a contract.

concepts.caption: The face size printed on the contract - not the price you paid for it.
concepts.definition: The face amount a derivative is written on — not what you paid.
concepts.example: An option on $100,000 of stock might cost $2,000. Notional is $100k. Premium is $2k.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Notional is the size of the underlying. Premium is what you paid for the contract.

concepts.caption: The ticket price of the contract. This is what protection costs.
concepts.definition: What you pay for an option — the price of the insurance.
concepts.example: That put costs $3 a share. The $3 is the premium.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Premium is the price of the contract. Yield is what an investment pays you over time.

concepts.caption: What the investment pays you, measured as a percent of its price.
concepts.definition: What an investment pays you, as a percent of its price.
concepts.example: A $100 bond that pays $5 a year yields 5%. Price falls to $50, yield is 10%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Yield is the income rate. Duration is how much the price jumps when rates move.

concepts.caption: The rate bruise: how hard the price jumps when interest rates move.
concepts.definition: How sensitive a bond's price is to interest-rate changes, in years.
concepts.example: A 10-year duration bond drops about 10% if rates rise 1%. That's the rate bruise.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Duration is the bruise from rate moves. Yield is the coupon you collect.

concepts.caption: Two lines that were supposed to move together, drifting apart.
concepts.definition: When your hedge doesn't move 1-for-1 with what you were trying to protect.
concepts.example: You hedge airline stock with an oil future. Oil falls, the stock doesn't. The hedge missed.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A hedge is the protection. Basis risk is the gap when that protection doesn't track.

concepts.caption: You own it and you want it higher.
concepts.definition: You own it, or you're betting it goes up.
concepts.example: You bought 50 shares. You're long. You want the price higher.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Long = you want it up. Short = you want it down.

concepts.caption: The weather report: how hard the price swings, not where it ends up.
concepts.definition: How violently the price swings — the weather, not the direction.
concepts.example: A stock that rips 8% some days is more volatile than a utility that moves 0.3%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Volatility is how hard one thing swings. Diversification is owning several so one swing doesn't sink you.

concepts.caption: Many baskets, so one dropped basket does not take the eggs.
concepts.definition: Owning different things so one disaster doesn't take the whole pile.
concepts.example: 20 stocks across 5 industries vs. your whole net worth in one employer.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Diversification spreads bets. A hedge is insurance on a bet you already have.

concepts.caption: The person standing on the other side of the contract, owing you.
concepts.definition: The other person in the contract — the one who has to pay you.
concepts.example: You bought a put from Bank X. Bank X is your counterparty. If they fail, the put is a napkin.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Counterparty is who sits across from you. Default is them failing to pay.

concepts.caption: The promise snaps: the payment they owed never arrives.
concepts.definition: Not paying what you owe, on a loan or a contract.
concepts.example: The company misses a bond payment. That's default. Bondholders may seize assets.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Default is a missed payment. Mark-to-market is just re-pricing the position while it's still alive.

concepts.caption: The price tag gets rewritten at today's number - sold or not.
concepts.definition: Re-pricing a position at today's market, even if you haven't sold.
concepts.example: Your $1M pledge is now worth $600k. The loan is marked to market. That's when the call comes.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Mark-to-market is a re-price. Default is a broken promise. You can be marked down and still paying.

concepts.caption: Your portfolio, pledged for cash - with a nicer name on the term sheet.
concepts.definition: A loan that uses your portfolio as collateral. You keep the shares.
concepts.example: $10M stock, 30% haircut, $7M loan. You didn't sell, so you didn't trigger capital gains — yet.
concepts.mixUpWhy: It's a pledge of securities for a loan. Pledge is the move; this is the product with a nicer name.

concepts.caption: The tax bill that only appears when you actually sell.
concepts.definition: The taxable profit when you sell an asset for more than you paid.
concepts.example: Bought at $1M, sell at $4M. $3M is a capital gain. A loan is not a sale.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Capital gains hit when you sell. Buy-borrow-die is the pattern of never selling so the tax doesn't trigger.

concepts.caption: Buy, borrow against it, never sell. The pattern, not advice.
concepts.definition: Buy assets, borrow against them to spend, hold until death so heirs may get a stepped-up basis. A tax pattern — not a plan we recommend.
concepts.example: Owns $2B of stock, borrows $20M a year against it, never sells. A crash can still force a sale.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A securities-backed loan is the borrowing tool. Buy-borrow-die is the whole life-cycle pattern that uses that tool.

concepts.caption: A promise with a date on it. Come December, you settle. No walk-away.
concepts.definition: A contract to buy or sell something at a set price on a set date — obligation, not a right.
concepts.example: Agree now to buy 1,000 barrels at $80 in December. Come December, you settle. You cannot walk away like an option.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Futures are a promise you must keep. An option is a right you can abandon.

concepts.caption: Two payment streams crossing: fixed on one side, floating on the other.
concepts.definition: Two parties exchange cash flows — often a fixed rate for a floating one.
concepts.example: You pay 4% fixed, receive SOFR. If rates jump, the swap pays you. That's a rate hedge, not a loan.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A swap is an ongoing exchange of payments. A future is one settlement on one date.

options.text: What you pay for the contract — the price of the insurance.
The face size of the underlying.
What a bond pays you each year.
The gap when a hedge doesn't track.

prompts.why: Premium is the price of the contract. Yield is what an investment pays you over time.

prompts.story: An option on $100,000 of stock costs $2,000. The $100,000 is the ____.
prompts.why: Notional = $100k. Premium = $2k. Mixing them makes a cheap option sound like a $100k bill.

prompts.story: That put costs $3 a share. The $3 is the ____.
prompts.why: You pay the premium. You do not pay the notional unless you exercise into the stock.

prompts.story: You try to sell $2M of a tiny stock. The bid vanishes. You get filled $80k lower than the last print. Apple would not have done that to you.
prompts.why: Ease of exit. Notional would be a contract size. This was the market refusing to catch your sale.

prompts.stem: The premium of an option is the same as its notional.
prompts.why: Premium is the ticket price. Notional is the stadium. $2k vs $100k.

pairs.right: Can you leave without a bruise?
Why you might buy that option

prompts.why: You buy a $2k premium on $100k notional as a hedge — if you can actually trade it. That's liquidity.

options.text: What an investment pays you, as a percent of its price.
How much a bond's price jumps when rates move.
What you pay for an option.

prompts.why: Yield is the income rate. Duration is how much the price jumps when rates move.

options.text: How sensitive a bond's price is to interest-rate changes, in years.
The coupon divided by the price.
The face size of a swap.

prompts.why: Duration is the bruise from rate moves. Yield is the coupon you collect.

options.text: When your hedge doesn't move 1-for-1 with what you were trying to protect.
Owning too many of the same stock.

prompts.why: A hedge is the protection. Basis risk is the gap when that protection doesn't track.

prompts.stem: Higher yield always means higher duration.
prompts.why: Often the opposite vibe: a fat current yield can sit on a short-duration bond. Duration is rate sensitivity, not the coupon.

prompts.story: A 10-year ____ bond drops about 10% if rates rise 1%.
prompts.why: That's the bruise. Yield is what it was paying you while you waited.

prompts.story: Airline. You worry about oil. You buy oil futures as a 'hedge.' Oil crashes. Ticket prices barely move. The futures lose money. The stock does not rally enough to save you.
prompts.why: You had a hedge. It didn't track. That's basis risk, not 'hedges are fake.'

prompts.story: A $100 bond pays $5 a year. Price falls to $50. New buyers now earn 10% on that same $5.
prompts.why: Income over price. Duration would tell you how hard that price fall was when rates moved.
Four words journalists stack. Pull them apart: income, rate-pain, a sloppy hedge, and the ticket for a put.

prompts.stem: If a hedge is perfect, basis risk is roughly zero.
prompts.why: Perfect 1-for-1. In real life you get close and hope. The leftover is basis risk.

prompts.stem: A tiny stock that cannot absorb a $1M sale has poor:
prompts.why: Ease of exit. Duration is a bond's rate-bruise, not a traffic jam in the shares.

prompts.story: Swap written on $50M of loans. You didn't pay $50M. That $50M is ____.
prompts.why: Face size. Premium would be what an option on that pile costs.

prompts.story: Rates jump 1%. Your long bond fund is suddenly down about 12%. The manager mutters a number in years.
prompts.why: Rate sensitivity. Yield is what it was paying. The 12% bruise is duration doing its thing.

prompts.stem: Paying a premium for a put is the same as earning yield on a bond.
prompts.why: Premium is money you spend for a contract. Yield is money an asset pays you.
If a sentence in the Journal has two of these, slow down.

prompts.story: Unit 1 callback. You own the stock. You buy a put. The put is imperfect — it tracks an index, not your name.
prompts.why: Still a hedge. The leftover mismatch is basis risk.

options.text: Yield is income. Duration is rate sensitivity.
They are two words for coupon.
Duration is what you pay for a put.
Yield measures how fast you can sell.

prompts.why: Income vs bruise. Keep them in different pockets.

prompts.story: Crash insurance on your shares costs $4. That $4 is the ____.
prompts.why: Ticket price of the put. Notional would be the size of stock it covers.

options.text: You own it, or you're betting it goes up.
You borrowed it and sold it.
You pledged it to a bank.

prompts.why: Long = you want it up. Short = you want it down.

options.text: How violently the price swings — the weather, not the direction.
A bet that it only goes up.
The other person in the contract.

prompts.why: Volatility is how hard one thing swings. Diversification is owning several so one swing doesn't sink you.

options.text: Owning different things so one disaster doesn't take the whole pile.
Insurance on a single bet you already have.

prompts.why: Diversification spreads bets. A hedge is insurance on a bet you already have.

prompts.stem: Diversification is just a fancy word for a hedge.
prompts.why: Spreading bets vs. insuring one bet. 20 stocks is diversification. A put on your Tesla is a hedge.

prompts.story: You bought 50 shares. You're ____. You want the price higher.
prompts.why: Long = own / want up. Short = borrowed and sold / want down.

prompts.story: Two funds. Same +8% year. One got there in a straight line. The other halved twice and recovered.
prompts.why: Weather, not destination. Diversification is how many names, not how jumpy one path was.

prompts.story: Your entire net worth is one employer's stock. A product recall hits. There is no put. There is no second industry.
prompts.why: One pile. One disaster. A hedge could have helped that one name; diversification would have meant other names too.
Direction, weather, and whether one storm can take the farm.

options.text: The other person in the contract — the one who has to pay you.

prompts.why: Counterparty is who sits across from you. Default is them failing to pay.

options.text: Not paying what you owe, on a loan or a contract.
Re-pricing the position at today's market.
The other bank in the trade.

prompts.why: Default is a missed payment. Mark-to-market is just re-pricing the position while it's still alive.

options.text: Re-pricing a position at today's market, even if you haven't sold.

prompts.why: Mark-to-market is a re-price. Default is a broken promise. You can be marked down and still paying.

prompts.stem: If your loan is marked to market after a drop, that automatically means you defaulted.
prompts.why: Marked down ≠ default. Default is when you miss the payment or the call. The mark is just the new number.

prompts.story: You bought a put from Bank X. If Bank X fails, the put is a napkin. Bank X is your ____.
prompts.why: Who sits across from you. Default is the failure itself.

prompts.story: The company skips a bond payment. Lawyers. Maybe seizing assets. The price already fell last month when people guessed this was coming.
prompts.why: The earlier price drop was a mark. The skipped payment is default.

prompts.story: Your $1M pledge is now worth $600k. Nobody missed a payment yet. The loan desk still re-values the collateral tonight.
prompts.why: A re-price. The margin call may follow. Default is only if the promise actually breaks.
Person, broken promise, new number, and the phone call the new number triggers.

prompts.stem: If you are long a stock, you want it to fall.
prompts.why: Long = up. Short = down. The oldest mix-up in the paper.

prompts.story: Your beautiful put is with a bank that just hit the news for all the wrong reasons.
prompts.why: The other person. If they default, the contract's model price is a postcard.

prompts.story: 8% days vs 0.3% days. That's ____, not a forecast of direction.
prompts.why: Weather. Diversification is how many roofs, not how hard the wind blows on one.

prompts.stem: A put on one stock vs. 30 different stocks:

options.text: Put is a hedge. 30 names is diversification.

prompts.why: Insurance on one bet vs. not making one bet the whole farm.
Four Journal words. None of them mean each other.

prompts.story: Pledged stock, Unit 1 style. Price drops. Desk revalues tonight. Tomorrow they may call.
prompts.stem: Tonight is ____. Tomorrow may be a margin call.
prompts.why: Re-price first. Call second. Default only if you don't meet it.

options.text: Default is a broken promise. Mark-to-market is a new price.
They are synonyms on loan desks.
Default is a type of put.
Mark-to-market means the other bank vanished.

prompts.why: You can be marked down and still current. Default is the miss.

prompts.story: Bought it, still holding it, want it higher: you're ____.
prompts.why: The boring, correct word. Short is the other seat.

prompts.story: You borrow 100 shares and sell them at $50, hoping to buy back cheaper. Your friend just buys 100 shares at $50 and keeps them.

options.text: Long. She owns the shares and wants them up.
A put — insurance on shares she owns.
A hedge — she sold to offset a risk.

prompts.why: She bought and holds: long. Borrow, sell, hope to buy back cheaper — that's your move, short. Up is the direction that hurts you.

options.text: A loan that uses your portfolio as collateral. You keep the shares.
Selling the portfolio to harvest losses.
A put on the whole account.
A swap of dividends for a fee.

prompts.why: It's a pledge of securities for a loan. Pledge is the move; this is the product with a nicer name.

options.text: The taxable profit when you sell an asset for more than you paid.
The interest on a securities-backed loan.

prompts.why: Capital gains hit when you sell. A loan is not a sale. That's the whole trick — and the whole risk.

options.text: Buy assets, borrow against them to spend, hold until death so heirs may get a stepped-up basis. A pattern, not a plan we recommend.
A strategy this app is telling you to use.
Selling every year to lock in gains.

prompts.why: A securities-backed loan is the borrowing tool. Buy-borrow-die is the life-cycle pattern that uses that tool. Description ≠ advice.

prompts.stem: This lesson is recommending you pledge stock and never sell.
prompts.why: No. We're naming a pattern wealthy people use, including the ugly part: a crash can still force a sale. Not advice.

prompts.story: Bought at $1M, sell at $4M. The $3M is a ____. A loan against the $4M is not a sale.
prompts.why: Tax (sometimes) follows the sale. The loan follows a pledge. Different doors.

prompts.story: $10M stock. 30% haircut. Bank offers $7M. Shares stay yours. You spend the $7M. No sale. Yet.
prompts.why: Unit 1's pledge, in private-bank clothing. Same margin-call risk if it drops 40%.

prompts.story: Person owns a giant concentrated position. Borrows against it for living costs. Never sells. The pitch is: heirs get a reset. The footnote is: one crash plus a call can dump the shares into a taxable event anyway.
prompts.why: Nickname for a tax pattern. The footnote is the Unit 1 margin call. We are not selling the pitch.
Pretty name, old move, tax reason, crash ending. Hold all four.

prompts.stem: Taking a loan against stock is the same as selling it for tax purposes.
prompts.why: Usually not — that's why the pattern exists. A forced sale after a margin call *is* a sale. The tax shows up when you didn't want it.

options.text: A promise to buy or sell at a set price on a set date — obligation, not a right.
The right to walk away after paying a premium.
An exchange of interest payments over years.

prompts.why: Futures are a promise you must keep. An option is a right you can abandon.

options.text: Two parties exchanging cash flows — often a fixed rate for a floating one.
A single settlement on one date for a barrel or a bushel.
The right to sell stock at a floor.
A portfolio pledged to a bank.

prompts.why: A swap is an ongoing exchange of payments. A future is one settlement on one date.

prompts.stem: You can let a futures contract expire unused, like an option, and only lose the premium.
prompts.why: No walk-away. Futures mark to market. You settle. Options are the ones you can abandon.

prompts.story: Agree now to buy 1,000 barrels at $80 in December. Come December, you settle. That's a ____ contract.
prompts.why: Obligation on a date. An option would have let you shrug if $80 became a bad idea.

prompts.story: You pay 4% fixed, receive SOFR. If rates jump, it pays you. That's a ____, not a loan.
prompts.why: Ongoing payments. A future would be one settlement. A loan would be principal you owe.

prompts.story: Farmer locks a sale price for harvest. Buyer locks a purchase price. Neither of them has an option to bail because the weather was weird.
prompts.why: Obligation. If they wanted the right to bail, they'd have paid a premium for options.

prompts.story: Company has a floating-rate loan and hates the uncertainty. It enters a contract: it will pay fixed, receive floating, for five years. No barrels. No expiration Friday.
prompts.why: Exchange of cash flows over time. A future is one date, one settlement.
All three are derivatives. The mix-up is which one lets you walk, which one you must keep, which one drips payments.

prompts.stem: A swap is just a futures contract with a friendlier name.
prompts.why: Futures: one date. Swaps: an ongoing exchange. Related family, different choreography.

prompts.story: Private bank, concentrated stock, cash without a sale. Unit 1 is whispering 'pledge.'
prompts.stem: The product name on the term sheet is:
prompts.why: Pretty label on a pledge. Haircut and margin call still live here.

options.text: A tax pattern some wealthy people use. A crash can still force a taxable sale. Not advice.
A free lunch this app endorses.

prompts.why: We describe it because you'll read it. We do not hand you the keys.

prompts.story: Right vs obligation: an option you can drop. A ____ you must settle.
prompts.why: That's the fork from Unit 2, grown up.

prompts.stem: If a margin call forces a sale of pledged stock, capital gains can show up even if you never wanted to sell.
prompts.why: That's the ugly footnote. The pattern assumes you never sell. The market does not assume that.
Two borrowing words, two derivative words. Don't let the nickname do the thinking.

prompts.story: Airline wants to lock jet-fuel economics without taking delivery of tankers each month. It exchanges payments tied to a fuel index for years.
prompts.why: Ongoing exchange. A future would be dated lots. A put would be crash insurance with a premium.

prompts.stem: The through-line of this whole game:

options.text: Hedge protects. Pledge borrows against. Same asset, different fork.
Futures are a kind of pledge.

prompts.why: If you leave with one sentence, take that one.

prompts.story: Loan against stock: usually no sale, so usually no ____. Forced sale after a call: hello tax.
prompts.why: Tax follows the sale. The call can create the sale you were avoiding.
